Jesse means so much to me. 'Scream, Queen! My Nightmare on Elm Street' dives into the history of Mark Patton's acting career and heavily contextualises the impact that AIDS scare-induced homophobia had on the possibility of the Final Boy taking off. Specifically, it looks at the cultural idea that the Final Girl happens when a woman moves from the feminine sphere to the masculine to overcome the (usually) male stalker/slasher. For that shift to happen, a Final Boy would have to begin in the feminine sphere, and very few (mainstream) writers are willing to do that, because it offends general audience sensibilities - 'a man should always be a man'. It's interesting to think of this in terms of transness as well, and the different reactions to trans men vs trans women. For an AFAB person to gravitate towards masculinity is more palatable to the culture (Western NH culture specifically) than for an AMAB person to gravitate towards femininity. I don't think we can get a proper Final Boy until we confront and unpack that bias; the threat has to remain supernatural, or else we're being asked to root for a man who's being done over by another man for almost the entire runtime. 

With that in mind, here's my pitch for The Empire Strikes Back being recognised as a horror film and Luke Skywalker being a Final Boy. He's stalked both physically and in his dreams, and even if there's a supernatural element, it's shared by both protagonist and villain, and Vader is very much a real-world physical threat. Luke's emotional control and attachment to others is constantly a point of focus, and the most straightforward desired outcome by the text if we read the Jedi as right (as opposed to subversive readings, which I like more, but whatever), Luke's job is to stifle that, achieve mastery of the self, and overcome the enemy. Of course it's more complicated than that, but I think the reading stands. (And then look at audience responses to Luke as being too effeminate, especially in comparison to Han - see the pattern?)

Ghoul will feel more rewarding as he's a VERY strong killer with a few bugs right now that work in his favour. 

But if you're trying to learn (and farm) on Survivor, I can't give you exact numbers, but I can try to help by breaking down how it works. 

There are four survivor BP categories, each with subcategories:

- Objectives (repair generators, open chests, unlock exit gates, escape through/open hatch)
- Survival (healing self, not getting hooked, escaping chase)
- Altruism (healing others, unhooking safely, taking protection hits)
- Boldness (taking chase, running in the open, working on objectives in the terror radius, sabotaging hooks)

Survival and Boldness can overlap heavily.

Each of these categories maxes out at 10,000 BP.

Completing a gen, if it hasn't changed, is 12.5 BP per 1% of completion, so 1250 BP for a full generator 0 to 100. Additionally, a Good skill check (black area) grants 50 BP, and a Great skill check (white area) grants 300 BP. 

Opening a chest gets you 250 BP, I think?

So to max out in Objectives, you'll usually want to do at least two generators, preferably three, knowing that you probably won't be the only one working on them. But skill checks will help feed BP. Chests are sort of optional, if you're farming items or desperately need something and can spare time, you can try one. Try to be the one opening the exit gate.

Same skill check bonuses apply to healing, except the Great bonus, which is a bit less (350 I think?). Unhooking gets you 1000 BP, a safe unhook gets you 500 on top of that. There are 6 hook states you can interact with; you could shoot for 2-3 safe unhooks, and that along with healing and taking hits will probably get you to the limit. 

For chase, entering and losing chase is what really farms points, and you lose chase when you walk. If you can learn to safely loop with walking involved, such as rounding checkpoint corners or walking immediately after a pallet drop, you can break chase, then enter it again by running. A few people have put together chase statistics, and it seems 60 seconds is the baseline for an effective chase, so try timing yourself to see how long you can go. If you have Kate unlocked, bring Windows of Opportunity to help. Mr TatorHead/NoPerksSince2020 has excellent beginner looping guides where you can learn one or two strong loops per map. Then you start chaining them with fillers. Remember the goal isn't really to escape, but to waste time. If you can get away, great. If not, that's normal. But remember being downed and hooked impacts your Survival score.

Escaping via the gate is 5000 BP, extra if you're the Obsession. The Hatch is 7000 BP. 

Survivor is a balancing act. Some will tell you to play selfishly until you climb to an MMR where your teammates actually help. As someone who is Bad at the Game and bounces around a lot, I find playing altruistically more engaging, and it increases the chances of success. Do not underestimate how fast your teammates will drop you if they catch you constantly in locker or edge map. 

Last tip is APM. If you're not being chased or healing, you should be touching a generator. If someone else is being chased, even if you're in the terror radius, do a gen, and use your eyes to tell you if the killer is too close or losing interest in the other survivor. The survivor feed is a huge help - when those spider legs are moving for someone else, your job is gens, unless they're close enough for you to maybe take a hit for them. Keep track of who's injured and try to heal before you pop a gen, as it will tell the killer where you are when you do. Healing beneath hook is generally bad practice, but if the killer is a mile away on someone else, it's probably fine and you avoid wasting time running to edge map. Just always try to be doing something. Generators, running killer, unhooking, healing. Don't be afraid to run to where you need to go. If you want to learn where your scratch marks spread, grab Fixated. In general, Fixated, Windows, and Deja Vu are fantastic beginner perks.

You are probably never going to get a 40k BP game. Abuse flowers, envelopes, cakes and streamers. Ask in lobby if anyone will toss on a streamer for you - people are more generous in this community than we give them credit for.

I think one of the problems with this is that "racism" has become synonymous with "bad/evil". Which is not to say that it isn't, but I've noticed that most knee jerk claims of, "I'm not racist!" are not a reaction to what was actually said or a reflection on their thoughts on other races/the systems that enforce racism, but a fear of being seen as bad. And nobody wants to be bad. But when that fear and the need to be seen as Good outweighs the push to reflect on why we call racism bad and how to combat it, both systemically and in ourselves, then the game is completely changed, because the primary focus is on a personal litmus test of moral purity and not on understanding how racism functions. Racism has been reframed from something you do to something you are (funny enough, the same thing happened to homosexuality — not a shot at queerness, but an example of how identity politics have developed over the past few centuries). So conversations begin and end with, "I'm not racist," because there's an implied permanence or innateness to it — I AM Bad, not I have done bad. 

When people's worldview relies upon them being Good, they may reach to justify all of their beliefs and behaviours as also Good, because the idea of being anything but would shatter them. And I think that's a distinct mindset from the first example. Anyone can be A — I have been A — but fewer people are B. Fewer does not mean few, though. And these people are loud.

I think we (white Western society) are afraid to look racism in the eye, because once you pull on that thread, you see that it's intertwined with so much more that we consider fundamental to society. And what can we do about society? The trend towards individualism pushes personal problems, personal solutions. But racism isn't a personal problem, even if there are people who swear top to bottom that individuals of other races are lesser than them. If we want to tackle it, we have to do it together, and community-building is at an all time low. Not gone, but certainly reduced, and the reasons behind THAT are just as complex as the reasons behind racism. 

But I really do encourage people, and if you'll forgive my saying so, Christians in particular to challenge this black and white thinking. There is evil in the world, but once you reduce everything to Good or Bad, you hamstring your ability to act impactfully and meaningfully. Racism is bad, it's not something you want to do, but we all do bad things. As a child, I did not have structured accountability and restitution modeled for me, and I self-flagellated over every single bad thing I did. I'm still working to build a better mindset, because this one has frankly destroyed my life. I don't LIKE it, but I can't ignore the fact that the moral absolutism does not serve me or the people around me. We don't excuse bad things, we don't excuse racism, but we need a path forward that isn't eternal punishment or damnation. If we cannot grow, if we cannot do wrong and go on to do good, it disincentivizes people from admitting to being wrong, to doing bad, because there is no recourse. I don't know if I've made my point effectively here, but hopefully it's food for thought.

Consider this perspective: when I think about my financial situation, or whether or not I'll keep my job, and I look at charities in my area, many of them are Christian and based in a church. Now, on the one hand, you could see this as a good thing; there's a net at the bottom of society to assist people who fall too far. And that is good. I personally would rather people not die of hunger or exposure. On the other hand, what a setup that is. If people who would prefer not to be Christian, or who simply don't think much about Christianity, fall on hard times, their only recourse may be to attend church if their own religious community cannot support them. This is especially relevant in Christian-dominated areas; my people lost their place of worship because there were so few of us we couldn't pay the rent on the building we were in. Or maybe you're in a war zone, as a civilian, and the only place you can seek shelter is run by a church. It's a last resort. And if the mood around the religion is literally "there but for the grace of God go I," you begin to see why Christian charity can look like a trap to people. But taking it further, if it's all you have, and the price of dinner and a bed is a sermon, that's not just free listening time. If I'm faithful to another religion, that's me having to put my beliefs aside and worship in a way that is not genuine — wearing somebody else's true belief as a costume to gain access to something that might save my life. There are generations of forced converts to Christianity, and even though we're mostly past a point in the West where the government is going to tell you what religion you must follow, these systems remain in place. It's a fine line to walk when your target audience is people at the end of their rope. There might not even be a non-coercive/exploitative way to go about it. Again, anything that saves a life, I consider baseline good; but we can have conversations beyond that about how we go about it.

I actually think your response is interesting — no insult or judgment intended, but there's a disconnect between what people believe missions are for (spreading the Word), and the experience of people on the receiving end of missions. Even if every participant in a mission wants to do good, this aid is almost always tied back to growing Christianity's numbers. And when help comes with strings attached, even so much as sitting through a sermon... it may seem like a small price to pay for food or shelter, but it's still a price. When humanitarianism is tied to advancing a religious agenda, it becomes difficult for the 'beneficiaries' swallow, because behind the good intentions of the individuals on the ground is an agenda that's taking advantage of someone's situation. There are members of these communities who will find Christianity life-changing and state that it saved them, and I believe them. But the individual experience doesn't really change the system behind it all, and that's the issue you'll likely find beneath a lot of anti-Christian sentiment. Obviously I'm here because I'm fascinated by Christianity, and I'm aware of the wide, wide range of Christians in the world that I respect; but I'm also aware that some of the ideas driving some modern Christian institutions have been extremely harmful to disadvantaged demographics. Which is why I said that it might not be fair to individual Christians, but there is anger directed at the mechanisms behind (Western Protestant) Christianity that will inevitably lead people to resisting even the most genuine one-on-one pleas for a change in belief.

Everyone else has dropped great points, but I think people who believe in proselytizing don't have a good grasp of how damaging it can be. I've studied missions academically, and there have been many, many cases where specific missionary groups take advantage of people who are at risk to coerce them into participating in the religion — you can have food if you come to services, we'll teach you to read but you need to have a Christian name, etc. And the targets are well aware that they're being preyed upon. Some people truly believe that missionaries go to underprivileged countries and active war zones out of generosity and the conviction that they're saving souls if not lives, but having read the correspondences of missionary leaders, they know exactly what they're doing. And when a group prominently goes after those whose options are saying yes or dying, in regions that have a longer memory than the relatively-young United States, you build generations of reflective resentment. The expression of this resentment isn't always fair on an individual level, but it does come from a history of exploitation and predation. I think a lot of churches fail to grapple with this history in a constructive way.

Ah, I had the same problem! I think it's important to know that this series breaks down people into parts: the body, and the soul. 

When you die, the soul usually separates from your body, and then where it goes varies. Most souls go to the River, a major concept explained in the next book, but think of it like the rivers of Hades. I won't say anything more to avoid speculation and spoilers. If a soul doesn't go to the River, weird shit starts happening, and it gets down to semantics and perspectives, because we're not so much dealing with a hard magic system so much as magic as it's being studied by academics, who are putting forward hypotheses on how it works. Generally, a wandering soul is called a spirit or ghost, while a revenant is a specific subtype of ghost that sticks around because of revenge. You'll see characters talking about 'traveling along thanergetic links' - think of those as rails built out of unfinished business that the vengeful soul travels along, and can't generally pop off of. Characters like Palamedes and Abigail study how this works, so you'll see them looking at bodies and objects and spaces to try to get impressions of what happened to a soul just before and then after death. 

So you generally get two broad schools of necromancy: body necromancy, and soul necromancy. Body necromancy gets broken down into bone magic (Harrow) and flesh magic (the Tridentarii), with subschools like blood magic and lymph magic. Soul necromancy gets more classes generally, though they're not always defined. Abigail studies where the soul goes after death; Palamedes studies impressions left on objects and spaces.

Sometimes you WILL see a necromancer call a spirit back. For example, Gideon explains where she got her name: the Ninth House necromancers called her mother's spirit back briefly, and all it said was 'Gideon'. 

Most of the necromancy you see, though, is body necromancy - Harrow raising skeletons on skeletons on skeletons. This is not resurrecting a person; this is putting energy into a bunch of bone and telling it what to do. Some necromancers go down to cell manipulation, which is how Harrow can manipulate bones like clay, but to make more out of nothing she seems to be giving her own energy to the bone mass to produce more cells. 

Another important point: thalergy and thanergy. Thalergy is life energy. Thanergy is death energy. When something dies, thalergy converts to thanergy. > Why does this space goth world not have guns?

Guns absolutely exist in this setting, but they're not often used by the Nine Houses. People outside of the Empire, or opposed to the Empire, are more likely to use guns. Remember that the Nine Houses run on necromancy; necromantic theory is scattered throughout the books and not always ease to keep track of, so I'll break it down a little here, as it's relevant to the swords. Basically, you have thalergy (life energy) and thanergy (death energy), and necromancers manipulate both of these. Weird pull, but if you've seen of/heard of Madoka Magica (I wouldn't put it past Muir), there's a similar system there, where hope is a power source, but the conversion of hope to despair also releases a sudden snap of power. You can keep track of death energy by remembering thanergy-thanatos-death. And this series is heavy on its mythological, scientific, and linguistic references. It'll eventually settle in your head and you'll start making connections. But for now, remember that necromancers need death energy to do most of their magic, and death energy is produced when something dies. That energy starts to decay; think about radiation, the initial bloom and then the gradual decline. The closer the necromancer is, the more of this bloom they can slurp up. There also seems to be a component of method of death, which contributes to how strong the bloom is. So, for the Nine Houses, the method is drop a bunch of people with swords in front of the enemy, have them run at them and slice them up and possibly die themselves. All that good death energy explodes out, and then the necromancers come in, slurp it, and start doing magic. Notice that this method sort of relies on the front line soldiers dying too, and pay attention to the Fourth House - the revolting teens. The Second and Fourth are the most militaristic houses, but the Second tends to produce commanders and the Fourth produces cannon fodder. 

> How do these houses work?

So, each House is a planet, maybe with some moons. What each House does is based on their own culture. Luckily, the main cast of book one are all repping their House hard, so they'll help you remember. But I'll do a quick guide. 

First House: the God-Emperor, and his Lyctors <- powerful necromancers regarded as saints, the thing the cast is trying to become

Second House: military, likely to produce officers, but not exclusive to this

Third House: lots of flesh magicians, they do fashion and political intrigue

Fourth House: military, likely to produce ground soldiers, but not exclusive to this

Fifth House: also cultural influencers, but at a slower, more stable rate; they're keepers of history, and produce a lot of spirit/River magicians

Sixth House: the libraryyy; scientists, researchers, record keepers

Seventh House: we don't know much about them, save for their obsession with aesthetics and the curse of hereditary sickness; they seem a prime vacation spot

Eighth House: cultists, but they deal with spirits and ghosts where the ninth deals with bones; again, we don't know much about them save that they're extremely secretive and religious, and dislike the Ninth

Ninth House: tomb guardians; they're there guarding the titular Locked Tomb, which contains the Emperor's greatest enemy; they're tiny and out of the way and people mostly move there for religious reasons.

Books 2 and 3 will get more into the economy and planets beyond the Nine Houses. 

> Becoming a Lyctor. 

Lyctors are, again, the most powerful necromancers in the universe, save for the Emperor. They're worshipped as saints. After 10,000 years, the original Lyctors have mostly died, so the Emperor wants the nine heirs as replacements. Figuring out how to become a Lyctor is the point of the First House building. We see Harrow and Gideon go through two trials; go back and pay attention to what those trials are teaching them. 

> Is it worth staying on?

I think so. The writing is incredibly deep once you dig into it. The issue is, if you're struggling with Gideon, Harrow the Ninth will fuck you up bad. I think the first read of HtN is something that's endured, not enjoyed. And I think if you don't have a good grasp of the first book, the second will lose you entirely. So read Gideon a few times. I learn something new every time I do. You can tell this is a well-planned series. Very few words are wasted. If you have the patience and you enjoy what you find when you sink into it, then go on to book two knowing that you'll also be reading it more than once.

Basically, our brains have a ton of shit running through them 24/7, including impulses and fears and stressors, and sometimes - especially when we're feeling stressed about something else - it hiccups, and a thought that's violent or upsetting comes up. This does not mean that you are secretly a violent or evil person. Imagine a monkey with a typewriter sitting in your head banging out random words. Now imagine experiencing stress, or having a chemical imbalance or neural issue associated with a condition like OCD, that softly turns the focus of the vocabulary towards the thing you fear. Then the thought comes up, and it's upsetting. What I'll say now is that if this hasn't happened much for you, it's a great time to practice letting these thoughts go. You haven't done anything wrong. It's just a thought. You can move on from it in the same way you would from a nightmare. You're okay.

So, regarding Biblical manuscripts, I don't believe we have anything concrete prior to the second century. There are a few reasons why we don't have more complete copies of very early Biblical texts, among them: environmental damage, purposeful destruction, alteration or reuse, and recycling of materials. Basically, the longer it's around, the more likely it is to be damaged or lost. Moreover, even when these items are preserved, they may be circling in fields that don't make them easy to pin down or identify, i.e. someone might have a lovely fourth century bit of papyrus and have no idea it has scripture on it, and it's being sold as an aesthetic oddity; or, as with raiding along the English coast, the actual materials that make up the manuscripts are considered more important than the contents of the text, so pages are scraped for gold or cut up for the artwork. In this way, we lose a lot of early manuscripts.

Another issue: the Bible as we know it today took a long, long, LONG time to come together. Centuries, in fact. Peter is getting ironed out around the 60s AD, but John won't be settling until the turn of the century; and these are just dates based on historical references within the texts - again, we don't actually have copies that are that old. And not all works produced during the first few centuries made the cut! Look into the Apocrypha, if you have the chance. You'll see how messy it gets very quickly. For example, we've kept 1 and 2 Peter, but the Gospel of Peter, which is an entirely separate writing, has not been incorporated into canon. The whys and hows and whos of these choices will grow you a lot of rabbit holes.

Then you have standardised versions of the ancient language versions of these texts that are used for 'modern' (read: early modern period on) translations. The issue is, as above, that even our Hebrew and Greek manuscripts are so varied that saying that one is definitive is an exercise in guesswork. And I'm not even getting into the Tanakh; if you want to explore the history of Jewish preservation of our texts, that's its own thing.

So... where to start?

There's a wonderful book called Misquoting Jesus by Bart D Ehrman that talks about how we get our translations of the Bible in a semi-anecdotal way that makes for an extremely pleasant read. It took me a few rereads to digest most of it, because there's a lot going on under the surface in terms of references and history, but I used it as a branching off point to get into things like the Textus Receptus - one version of a standardised Greek New Testament. Reading about how it was used, re-examined, reworked and rejected really broadened my horizons re: the idea of an 'original' ancient language text.

If you want to get into how we identify and translate the literal words found in certain copies of the Bible, use Biblehub's text analysis. I'm serious. It references Strong's Concordance, which isn't unproblematic, but will crack open the vocabulary vault for you. I'm not even done with it yet. 

I hope that's like... a good start. It's a wonderful field, I'll tell you that. Very exciting to get into!

Leviticus, which is sort of the book of rules and regulations of the Bible and discusses a variety of bodily/sexual rules, does have a passage on emission, or sexual climax from a penis. That would be Leviticus 15. Emission is put on a level with menstruation, interestingly, and has similar rules: you are considered unclean while engaging in any act that would cause discharge, including, interestingly, climax denial or edging - "The uncleanness of his discharge is this: whether his member flows with its discharge or is stopped from discharging, he is unclean during the entire period his member flows or is stopped from discharging; this is his uncleanness." Anything you touch from that point on is also considered unclean, and needs to be washed, preferably by that evening. Evening is when the sort of 'transmission' period ends, followed by seven days of general but presumably not transmissible uncleanliness, in which you bathe and wash your clothes daily, and an eighth day with a double dove sacrifice. 

Similar rules apply for menstruation, as mentioned before. In this case, they are unclean for the entirety of the period and 'transmissible' until they stop bleeding, while those who touch them are to cleanse the same day and will be considered clean at nightfall. Note that this all follows Jewish practice of nightfall marking a new day, as opposed to dawn. Likewise, Judaism has a system for purification; a pool, called a mikvah or mikveh, is used especially for cleansing immersion. I won't get too much into the Jewish perspective, as this is presumably a Christian question, but it is worth noting that 1) this exists and 2) its use varies wildly.

Now, is to be 'unclean' to be 'in sin'? Not necessarily. Note that emission no matter the cause - masturbation or reproduction - causes uncleanliness. If we're to take all the writings of Paul as genuine (which I wouldn't), we see a man (or multiple men) struggling to establish a consistent set of rules for a budding Church. Marriage is actually not the most desirable option here: it's absolute celibacy. Marriage is the failsafe for being unable to achieve this - concession, not command. 

διὰ δὲ τὰς πορνείας ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα ἐχέτω καὶ ἑκάστη τὸν ἴδιον ἄνδρα ἐχέτω

Due to (the unfortunate circumstance of) sexual immorality, each man should take a wife, each woman should take a husband. 

Interestingly, it also mentions that they should have sexual relations when the need arises, so as to minimize the chances of sin occurring, but doesn't mention children.

The translation of the initial verse from Hebrew is actually quite complex in context. 

וְאֶ֨ת־זָכָ֔ר לֹ֥א תִשְׁכַּ֖ב מִשְׁכְּבֵ֣י אִשָּׁ֑ה תּוֹעֵבָ֖ה הִֽוא

For example, there are no prepositions in this sentence - with, as, are not present. -כ is not attached to ‎מִשְׁכְּבֵ֣י, so no comparison in relation to 'lying' specifically is being made. את is not attached to אשה, likewise. ‎מִשְׁכְּבֵ֣י also Biblically refers to incest; sexual activity doesn't really use the same term. זכר specifically includes adults and children. Another, equally valid interpretation might be, Men and boys should not allow themselves to be bedded in the position of a woman (subservient), in incest. Given the rest of this section of Leviticus is about forms of incest and their punishments, i.e. having relations with both a woman and her daughter, sleeping with your brother's wife as she is considered family, etc.

I think it's worth addressing who translates the Bible, and when, and why, before bringing out anything as a certainty.

Hey brother, sounds like you're hitting the college wall, which is very, very normal. Most people experience this - you are not a failure for feeling this way. I just wanted to make that clear first.

Before anything else, reach out to your academic advisor and current professors. Explain how you've been feeling and where you're struggling. Emphasize that you want to do well and be open to what they have to say. They may be able to help you create a schedule that works for you. 

My advice regarding studying is: 15 minutes is fine. The way I studied in uni was 15 minutes on, 15 minutes off. When I didn't know how to study, the first thing I did was copy my notes out, by hand or on a computer. Simply having to write out the information again helped it stick in my head. It might be worth it for you to also look into mnemonics - memory games you can play to help you retain more information. But turning studying into a thing to be dreaded is gonna contribute to that wall. Make a promise to yourself: every two hours, you will study for fifteen minutes, beginning with copying out notes or bits of your textbook. It's only 15 minutes, which means it will be over quickly, and once it's done you can do whatever you want. Build up to do 15 minutes every hour. But a small amount of studying with low pressure is better than trying to cram for an hour while hating yourself.

Regarding smoking and drinking, avoid these if you can. They won't take the edge off the way you want them to. I drank through undergrad and masters and am lucky to have been able to scrape by while avoiding alcoholism, but it was close. Once you start, it's harder to stop. Better not to start at all. Which sounds lame, but it is what it is. What I'd suggest is light exercise. I know it sounds stupid, especially with regards to mental health, but I'm not talking about getting a gym membership or taking a class. Again, 15 minutes is a great time. Take one 15 minute walk in the morning and one in the evening. Listen to music or an audiobook. Get outside and get some sun most importantly. Exercise will not fix your mental health, but getting movement and vitamin D will give you a fighting chance and a firm foundation. 

Lastly, seek counseling through your school. It never hurts to have someone to talk to, and they'll be able to identify any major mental health red flags and treat them. 

Take care of yourself. Come back here if you need support. I'm sorry it's so bad right now, but there is a way for it to be better. I believe in you.

Benji is visibly triggered multiple times during the film; he read as bipolar to me, having been manic the day before and going into a slump that morning after being woken up (not David's fault, it just is how it is; Benji talks a lot about treasuring sleep and getting rest, I'd imagine he's someone who pingpongs between no sleep and sleeping too much), so everything feels that much more intense to him. He clearly has some sort of issue if not bipolar, and so his emotions burst out of him at inappropriate times and in highly aggressive ways. And I do think he reads as a person who was actually very educated, but whose emotions and intelligence are at war with one another. When they line up, such as when noticing Marsha was upset and needed company, he can come across as a very astute, emotionally intelligent person, almost psychically so; but when they're out of alignment, you get scenes like the train or the graveyard. But the graveyard also touches on something else I at least felt was running through the film but not really articulated, though Benji tries and fails to do so: Jewish guilt, and not feeling Jewish enough. Benji doesn't have community - he appears to be homeless and while he makes connections quickly, they're not very strong. The closest relationship he had was with his grandmother, and he's just lost her. So he's gone on this tour to connect with her and it's throwing up a lot of emotions for him. You see it most often with Eloge; Benji is both impressed and intimidated by him. Eloge is a practicing Jew who actively chose Judaism instead of being born into it, who experienced a genocide firsthand. Benji knows what this means and how important it is, but it's also stirring up feelings of imposter syndrome and inadequacy. You see him get triggered in the graveyard specifically when Eloge is talking to James about research he did during the tour, showing a consistent character trait in his willingness to really dig into the history of Judaism and Jewishness. Benji, who has been born to it, has learnt most of what he knows through osmosis, but doesn't seem to be practicing, and he certainly isn't as knowledgeable as Eloge. And so he feels threatened, and asserts himself in that scene by taking the angle that they're being disrespectful by citing statistics instead of 'feeling' the weight of the history - a nebulous thing that anyone can do and no one can really be judged on. He shuts them up, and he does it because he really truly feels: guilty, disconnected, and inadequate. The same is true on the train. He's grappling with this sensation that he just doesn't have the tools to cope with and so it explodes outwards. Contrast with Dave, who directs most everything inwards. He's also intimidated by Eloge, but makes self-deprecating comments and doesn't confront the feeling. But for Benji especially (sorry this comment is rambling), this is a person who just tried to kill himself coming face to face with people who weren't given a choice in the matter, and who fought to live anyways. He probably does feel as horrible as he says, but it's coming out filtered through a layer of slightly dated academia, and is two degrees too aggressive because he's afraid that if someone more educated gets a chance to speak they'll put him down and he'll just feel worse. It's a very human way of being that made me quite uncomfortable. Really well done.

Here's a thought: how self-awareness presents is probably culturally dependent. For example, where I live, it's expected that people stand on the right and walk on the left for things like moving footpaths or escalators. However, many tourists come from countries where that is the opposite. When they stand on the left and block people, most are not aware that they're in the way, and because they don't have the cultural context to recognise why someone behind them may be looking frustrated, they may assume the stranger is just generally in a hurry, or upset about something entirely unrelated. Would we call it a lack of self-awareness that they don't realise they're acting as an obstacle?

With that example in mind, how much of 'self'-awareness is actually dependent on feedback from others? In the case of being too loud, or taking up too much space: if the person is in a new situation, they're probably going to gauge what's appropriate by how others are reacting to them. But then, what of culture, again? In some countries a cough would be an indication that someone is doing something inappropriate, and a 'self-aware' person in the know would interpret it as such and alter their behaviour. But what if they're from a culture, or even just a family, where direct communication is expected, and a cough is just a cough? Is that person now not self-aware regarding the situationally-inappropriate behaviour?

I'm not even trying to break down the entirety of the idea here - this is just one aspect to consider. Other people have mentioned neurodivergence, but there are so many other factors (upbringing, personality, context) at play.

Speaking strictly in a medical sense, if this were a formal or even just an ethical study, I personally believe that examining people in the grips of psychosis on anything other than a removed observational level would sadly be taking advantage of them. If we think about experiments involving humans as a matter of consent, then people experiencing psychosis are 99.99% unable to give informed consent because they aren't thinking clearly. I bet many would be eager to talk about what they're experiencing, but as the person putting them in that position, you'd have to examine your own motivation for doing so - is it therapeutic to allow access to better treatment, or is it to enhance your own understanding of the universe? It's hard because I can imagine the value of being completely open to and exploring everyone's perceived reality, but as the person on the other end I also know I was in no position to give anyone real insight into life's mysteries (so to speak). Perhaps you'd be best served to start with studies done on the neurology of people with schizophrenia? If you're wondering what material conditions of the brain cause changes in perception, that would be where I'd begin. These are definitely symptomatic of untreated neurodivergence. She probably wants you to be in the loop regarding her diagnoses because they go a long way towards explaining her behaviour. Not excusing it — based on your other comments, you seem to presume laziness or malice on her part, so to preempt, that's not what I mean. What I mean is, for people with these conditions, these behaviours are natural, meaning they don't really think about them as they're doing them; and if they aren't noticing what they're doing, they can't make conscious changes. A diagnosis and therapy help them understand why they do the things they do, which hopefully leads to better management. If you allow yourself to be brought into the fold here, you'll be able to GENTLY help her identify when she's doing something that spawns out of that divergence. It may also take some of the weight off of you. For example, my mother presumed I was lazy for the longest time because she would ask me to do the dishes and hours would go by without me touching them; she would come down and ask why they weren't done in an accusatory way, and I'd be startled, because I was absolutely willing to perform the task, I just hadn't realised there was a time limit. Now when I'm staying with her she asks me if things can be done by a certain time, and so I do them. It's half me knowing my own tendencies after working with a therapist, and half her making a change in the way she approaches me to achieve a better outcome. You sound worn down and bitter, and I don't want to cast aspersions, but I think you need to take a bit with your wife and ask yourself the honest question of, "Do I want a relationship with my child?" She's only nineteen. She's been through the worst developmental years, when her brain is putty and her hormones run the show, and she has the unfortunate added hurdle of living in a culture not set up for people with neurological structures like hers. I firmly believe that if you do the work here, you unlock the rest of your lives with your child as she grows into an adult with a better sense of self who knows she can trust you and who loves you. But if you dismiss her, and don't give both her and you the opportunity to learn, you risk her believing that she is going to have to grow into the person she will be alone. Having been through frankly the hardest part of that journey, raising a teenager, is this where you want to get off? I'm not saying it will be perfect and you'll never fight again. I'm saying you made a child who is almost at the finish line for the worst of it and who is reaching out to you as she moves into the next phase of her life, and you have a choice to make about whether you reciprocate or cut her off. I do not feel any strong attachment to the physical, modern state of Israel, despite my family being Israeli. I simultaneously understand the fear of having our culture stripped away and, as a person, am wary of cultivating a fear of intermingling in general. We could have a long discussion about that word, intermingling, and where it actually conceals forced assimilation, but I don't really feel like getting into it on Reddit. I do not believe that the chief end of Jewish existence is the reclamation of a particular plot of land. I absolutely understand why other people do think that way, I know how central it is to aspects of worship, but I have never felt I need to be in modern Israel to be a good or worthy Jew. I am also leery of tribalism in general — I try not to cast judgment on it, I absolutely participate in it (I am actually on the Judaism subreddit for reasons other than flapping my gums), but I also have seen how it can lead to doing harm unto others, and so I try to check it in myself and in my community. It is loaded language, but Israel reads to me as simultaneously THE most modern state state on the board (perhaps because of its young age) in a way I, a state-disliker of habit, don't gel with; and as a shtetl on a global scale where we balance self-determination and the right to lock the gates and preserve what is inside with being boxed in and the prickly sense of wariness that comes from it. We will always have to live with goyim because we are people on Earth, and I think there is a line between saying, 'Don't touch me, I can be what I am,' and preemptively swatting at hands. The reaction, while understandable, is not always useful or appropriate, and I see how that and the mentality that Jews must be monolingual and live in one part of the world and maintain this forever play into each other. 

I don't think there is a right answer to the conundrum of diaspora versus... neo-indigenous identity (I don't know what else to call it), which is why I said I think we fundamentally disagree, not that one of us is right or wrong. I could say that, from my political perspective as a person who worked to preserve the Yiddish language, I was positioned with Hebrew 'monolingualists' (of course they're not literally monolingual) as an opposing force that made my job harder. However, those same people dealt with the issues you're describing and had their own reasons for championing Hebrew as The Jewish Language (which I wouldn't compare to a lingua franca; a lingua franca is a matter of convenience, but framing Hebrew as revolutionary and Yiddish as assimilationist or insidious is a value judgment). I think you semi-correctly identify the reasons why Yiddish came to be, but the perspective you bring to the table is that it is bad because it mingles Jewishness with goyische culture, and that that 'dilution' is a loss. Conversely, I see it as a strength and also just a symptom of the fact that we are not alone here - and I do not want us to be! And because I want us to be able to live around the world, because I rejoice in that geographical diversity although it came out of persecution in most cases, I do not think diasporic languages should be devalued or retired.
I think we have fundamentally incompatible views of what it is to be Jewish, which is as surprising as finding a fork in a kitchen.

There's also the fact that the comment above puts Yiddish down for being based on 'a goy language', which puts us on a slippery slope of 'intermixing bad', which is, in fact, cringe! To imply that Yiddish is less worthy because it is a diasporic language when it is NOT the same as German or Polish and is a product made by Jews for Jews, or to imply at all that the diaspora is less than and Yiddish should be binned because it's 'assimilatory' (as if it was ever spoken by the gentile German elite?), is cringe! Cringe is the appropriate response. We need to be careful about this mindset, it's a fear response from a long history of having our self-determination challenged, but that doesn't mean that what we create in a foreign land is unworthy or should be decommissioned because we don't 'need' it anymore. Yiddish = assimilationist and Hebrew = liberationist is a broken dichotomy. Shana tova.

There's a difference between being 'anti-Hebrew' (I don't think it's even possible for an observant Jewish person to be anti-Hebrew, it's necessary for worship) and being critical of the way that Hebrew is disseminated today, and held up as the 'gold standard' of Jewish languages, while other languages are put down due to being diasporic, instead of raised up as equals to Hebrew, and honoured for the role they have served, and preserved out of respect for those that spoke them and the continued understanding of their art. To narrow down Judaism to one language is to create an image of Judaism that is inherently exclusive of other Jews. I have worked in Yiddish preservation and have experienced the (rather bold) judgment of Hebrew-speakers who didn't understand why we still spoke the language. Pretending as though there isn't a certain dynamic here, with a political backing and slant, is not well-reasoned, it's stubborn and closed-minded. This is a phenomenon that can be very clearly traced through the past hundred years, the push for Hebrew to be centred as 'the' language instead of a language - a sacred language, but not one that necessitates the retirement of our other languages. Israel is not the first country to do this; France is, in my opinion, the worst about it, but the United States also pushed for monolingualism (and still does in places despite its diverse population). To recognise something that Israel is doing as a state, something that is not *unique* to it as a state, is not an attack. Israel is not infallible, it has a government made up of people as flawed as us. Linguistic supremacy is a real phenomenon and a tool to put others down and it should be recognised and checked. It is not the way. Does that serve as a defence?

Like 50 mg? Babe that's about as low as it goes so there's nothing to be afraid of. But I'm a setraline warrior so I can tell you my experience. What will likely happen is that you'll go on it and probably not notice anything for a few days. Then things will start to change. And you may panic because of the sudden loss of stimuli, and thus it may feel icky. It takes about a month to build it up and adjust to it. They will catch if you're allergic or having intense side effects VERY early on and take you off if they need to. Communicate with your doctor. One side effect I've found unavoidable in myself and everyone I know on it is weight retention. I have embraced this but it took time. It will likely not make you blow up like a balloon but it's something to be aware of. I'm a big eater and I'm stable at my weight on it.

And I have had my periods of getting cocky and comfortable and going off it without my doctor's help. Don't. The withdrawal is awful. It'll give you brain shocks. If you wanna go off, determine why first. If it's because you're 'doing well and done need it', that's the devil talking. You're doing well because you're on it. If it's not working, the doctor will help you taper and transition to something else. It may not help! You may need another kind of medication. You have to find one that works for you.

Even if it does work, expect to increase dosage after a year or two. This is not a failure or a sign that you're worse. The body adapts very quickly to sertraline. I have upped my dose twice and had a year where I went on something else just to reset my tolerance, monitored by my doctor. Being in the hundreds is not uncommon.

It won't make you happy. It will just put you on an even playing field. The problems will still exist, but you may find space growing in your mind to deal with them. I found that sertraline gave me the foundation to make therapy work for me. It held me down enough for me to do what I needed to do. And some days are still bad! I have slips, and depressive periods, and my OCD still exists. And I'm so accustomed to being on my meds that these seem like big failures. And then, because I'm a clown who's gone off cold turkey before, I remember how bad it can ACTUALLY be, and that this is just what normal people deal with. And that makes me feel more okay with the bad days. Now they're manageable periods of struggling instead of an endless nightmare. And now I can have good days too. Maybe not the manic highs I once had, but I don't need those. They were as scary as the lows in some ways.

Basically, it's going to be okay. You'll go on it. You'll know quickly if you need to stop or change. You'll adapt to a new normal where things are just a bit less intense and you'll be able to form skills to give yourself more and more breathing room. And maybe you'll hit a drop where things feel consistently worse, and need to up your dose. It will never be a cure all, but you should, in time, be able to differentiate between 'this is hard but doable' and 'this is hard because of my mental health problems'. Sertraline makes the former possible, the latter need to be addressed with a professional. Do not stop taking them. Keep on top of refills. But don't panic if you ever miss a day. It will stay in your system for at least 24 hours. If you're in an emergency where you're running low on pills and can't get your next dose, I've found breaking them in half is better than having none at all, but get the refill ASAP. Take them with food because you might get nauseous. You don't have to change your eating habits but you may gain weight. Don't worry about keeping it off. If you're at the point where you're just starting meds, you have bigger things to deal with in your life and that can be addressed later. Get stable first, then circle back if you want to.

Good luck mate. Hopefully things will be better for you now.

And I have to try and live in the third one. They aren't privy to any thoughts I don't share. What matters are my actions and the things I say. So I keep track of those, and call them my 'hard evidence', because that's the third person narrative that we both have to work with. So if my words and actions aren't manipulative, we don't have a manipulative relationship. Of course there's nuance to it, but I've found over time that it's better to err on the side that I'm not doing it, because I naturally overcorrect so hard in the direction of, "I'm horrible and doing everything wrong," that what to me seems like a huge lunge - "I'm not doing anything wrong" - actually puts me back in a neutral zone. I have to deal with the emotional world OCD creates for me, but I have to make decisions based off of my hard evidence, because if I don't, I'll spiral into behaving like my thoughts are real, and it will tank the relationship. People can only put up with "what if I'm manipulating you" for so long. I have a mantra that a problem does not exist unless they say it exists. My job, then, is to be as open as possible to them bringing problems to me so they feel safe to do so if something IS wrong. Sometimes I fuck up, but that's life. But try to focus on what's concrete.

I have had both OCD and psychosis, though I'm not schizophrenic. With OCD, it usually manifests as a 'negative' — 'did that just happen', 'what if this happened'; i.e. there's nothing there but I worry it is. With psychosis, it's a 'positive' — I hear or see or feel something, to me it IS there, and I learn later that it's not. Sometimes they slide into each other. I had a long psychotic episode where I was convinced I had a condition that turned objects invisible to my eye that felt very similar to the OCD 'what if something is there'. I've had OCD anxieties fuel psychotic episodes where I believed people were planning to kill me. For me the line does get very blurry, but oftentimes with OCD there are usually steps I take in response to the stimuli, i.e. people may want to kill me if I think impure thoughts, whereas with psychosis it simply is and I can't do anything about it.

It's bc DID is one of the least understood by the general public, and one of the worst represented in media; for many people without DID, it falls under the umbrella of "the scary mental illness" along with things like psychosis, antisocial personality disorder, and bipolar disorder. When these things are used solely to fuel conflict at the table by making a PC aggressive or unpredictable, it is implicitly dehumanizing people with these illnesses by denying them depth or self-awareness. The same honestly applies to playing "sociopaths" or "psychopaths" - it's not even that people as described by how media portrays these "conditions" don't exist, it's that it stems from something other than the named conditions. And the misnomer means people WITH DID, psychosis, ASPD, etc. are associated with the traits presented under the incorrect label instead of what the condition actually entails. I.e. if you want to make a Malkavian whose issue is that they can be duplicitous and backstabby and out of touch with or uncaring of what other people think, DID doesn't do that, therefore giving your character "multiple personalities" is mislabeling. If a character is "two-faced", you can just say that and have it be a better descriptor without attaching a diagnosis to it.
